title: Anthropic launches Claude Duet, a proactive agent that watches your apps and reports in
subtitle: Announced October 21 and running on Opus 5.5, the research-preview app sends a morning brief, checks connected apps every few hours, and asks before any consequential action.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Anthropic unveiled Claude Duet on October 21 as a standalone proactive-agent app for professionals and small-business owners. The app runs on Claude Opus 5.5, connects to a user's apps, sends a morning brief summarizing what matters, and then checks the connected apps every few hours for the rest of the day, pinging the user when something needs attention. Access is a waitlisted research preview for US Pro and Max subscribers through the web and an iOS app — Reuters' wire added Android to the list, though MacRumors' launch coverage limited availability to iOS and web, so treat Android as unconfirmed until Anthropic says so directly. Duet operates on its own but holds a hard approval gate: it asks before sending a message, making a payment, signing a document, or deleting a file.

The design matters more than the feature list. Most agent products sold through 2026 are reactive — the user asks, the agent acts. Duet inverts that: the agent watches first, then surfaces work. Opus 5.5 is doing the watching, which is Anthropic's current frontier model, and the always-on polling pattern means the model is spending tokens on a user's workflow whether or not the user is in the chat. That is a different business shape from the per-session paradigm the industry has used so far, and it explains the Pro/Max gating.

The move slots into a crowded field. OpenAI shipped Dots as a proactive layer earlier this quarter, and Meta's Muse line has been iterating on the same pattern since summer. Each lab is now betting that the next step past 'chatbot' is 'co-worker who notices things' — a surface that competes with email triage tools, personal-assistant apps, and parts of the project-management stack. The approval gate on consequential actions is the industry's current compromise between autonomy and trust; whether that gate holds under heavy daily use is the open question.

A takeaway for learners: proactive agents move the risk model. A reactive assistant is only wrong when you ask it something; a proactive one can be wrong by surfacing noise, by missing signal, or by taking an action you did not intend. If you are evaluating one for your own work, measure three things across a two-week trial — how often it interrupts you, how often the interruption was worth it, and how often you had to undo something it did. That ratio tells you whether the agent is helping or just adding a new inbox.
